Relative Clauses: Prepositions and Relative Clauses After Pronouns

Remember: Relative Clauses are clauses (sentences) that start with relative pronouns who, that, which, whose, where, and when.

Relative Clauses are used to clarify which person or thing we are talking about.
Examples:
This is the man who helped me during the project.
The dogs that love cats are special.
The beach was definitely the thing >, whichI enjoyed most about my holiday.
I met a girl whose husband is a pilot.
This is the company where I worked for 20 years.
I remember my graduation party.
It was the day when the earthquake happened.
As you can see, those relative pronouns provide extra or specific information about the people or things we are talking about.

There are rules about using prepositions in relative clauses and using relative clauses after pronouns.

When a preposition is needed in a relative clause, it can before the relative pronoun or at the end of the clause.

For example:

Science is a subject which I always had trouble with.
Science is a subject with which I always had trouble. (This structure is generally more formal)

There are some fixed prepositional phrases you can use in non-defining relative clauses such as:</br><span class="italic"> in which case </br>at which point</br> as a result of which</br> the result of which was that</br> by which time

For example:

There was a scandal, as a result of which all the bosses resigned.

Defining relative clauses often follow these pronouns:

someone, anyone, something, anything, everything, all, many those, some, nothing, little, much

For example:

Many who saw the movie were amazed.

Body Language in the Workplace
Did you know that 95% of communication is nonverbal? This means that your body language has a great impact on the way people perceive you.

Having excellent non-verbal communication skills tells your audience (whether they be a group of people at a presentation, or an individual coworker) that you are confident, honest and motivated.  </br></br>Here are a few things to keep in mind about your body language at work:

1. Posture - how you feel affects how you stand. Stand tall, with your shoulders back and head up.
  2. Be in sync with others around you. Observe their body language and try to match it. That makes you appear interested and engaged.
  3. Eye contact. Being able to maintain eye contact with someone communicates confidence, authority and attentiveness.
  4. Show interest. Respond verbally and nonverbally to what others are saying.
  5. Try not to fidget. Fidgeting is interpreted as a nervous habit and most people are unaware they do it.

images.text: Observing your audience can be an extremely useful way to gauge interest levels during your presentation. If you have an idea of what gets their attention, you will not only be able to get a good idea of how effective your content is, but as a clear picture of how to engage with audience members from that point on.  A lot of the signals given off by body language are picked up intuitively, in which case, here are some basic things to look out for:

Facial Expressions
These are fairly self-explanatory. You might not always have a clear view of the audience's faces, but facial expressions can be extremely useful to determine audience reactions.
Leaning Forwards
A subconscious move to lean forwards towards the presenter is a classic indicator of interest whereas someone leaning back in their chair may be bored.
Crossing of Arms
Crossing the arms can be a defensive signal, or it can indicate disagreement. Audiences reacting in this way could be reacting to a touchy subject, or something that your audience isn't really happy with.

What is worth noting is that an audience member exhibiting any of the above actions is not always giving off these subconscious signals. If someone sat with their arms crossed throughout the whole presentation, it wouldn't necessarily mean they are offended by everything the presenter has said – this could simply be their preferred mode of comfort. And if someone else kept shifting around in their chair in an attempt to get comfortable, it wouldn't necessarily indicate anything.
If you observe the behaviour of the group as a whole, you are going to get a more accurate representation of the response to your presentation.
